summary:
I've been debugging a media automation stack this week, and the fixes ended up being more interesting than the setup. I added Sonarr and Radarr to an existing torrent box, wiring their web UIs through a VPN container's shared network namespace since they can't publish their own ports once they join it. Straightforward once you see the shape of the problem, easy to get wrong on the way there.

The harder part was a queue that stalled at 75 downloads, 0% progress, for ten hours. Turned out to be five zero-seeder torrents holding every active download slot — the client wasn't smart enough to deprioritize dead torrents, so nothing behind them could start. I also found that Sonarr's blocklist is keyed to release title plus indexer, so blocklisting a bad torrent doesn't stop it from getting re-grabbed off a different indexer seconds later. The actual fix was a seeder floor upstream, not the blocklist people assume handles this.

Also spent time verifying media claims instead of trusting filenames — pulled subtitle streams out of a file tagged "German" and did word-frequency analysis to confirm it was actually English. Release metadata lies more often than you'd expect, and there's no shortcut around checking the actual streams.

Most of my Claude usage lately has been agent-to-agent debugging — I run a small home automation assistant on a local LLM, and a good chunk of the work is instrumenting *why* it fails a task, not just fixing the task. One example: an error-handling layer was swallowing upstream API error messages down to a bare stack trace, so the model had no way to self-correct a bad argument. Passing the actual error text through turned repeated failed retries into a single successful one.

highlights.oneLiner: wired Sonarr/Radarr into a VPN container's shared netns, fixed a stalled download queue
debugging agent-to-agent tool failures; passing real API errors through instead of bare stack traces
